title: BSF Stops Akal Takht Jathedar's Zero Line Ardas for Kartarpur Corridor Reopening
excerpt: BSF stopped the Akal Takht Jathedar-led jatha from reaching the Zero Line at Dera Baba Nanak; the sangat held Rehras Sahib and ardas near the barricade as a Nagar Kirtan proceeded on the Pakistan side.
body:
• BSF personnel stopped Akal Takht Jathedar Giani Kuldeep Singh Gargajj and a jatha of Sikh devotees from reaching the Zero Line at Dera Baba Nanak on September 21, where they planned a special ardas seeking the Kartarpur Corridor's reopening.
  • Denied access, the sangat sat near the BSF barricade and held Rehras Sahib, Gurbani Kirtan and Ardas for the corridor's restoration and peace between India and Pakistan.
  • Across the border, devotees joined a Nagar Kirtan from Gurdwara Sri Darbar Sahib to the Zero Line; their kirtan could be heard on the Indian side.
  • The corridor has been suspended since May 7, 2025, after Operation Sindoor, and the MEA says the security situation still blocks reopening.

Border Security Force personnel stopped Akal Takht Jathedar Giani Kuldeep Singh Gargajj and the Sikh jatha accompanying him from reaching the Zero Line at Dera Baba Nanak in the Gurdaspur sector on September 21, blocking a planned special ardas by Sikh sangat from both sides of the border seeking the early reopening of the Kartarpur Corridor. The Jathedar and the devotees then sat near the BSF barricade and continued the religious program there.

The jatha had set out for the Zero Line at the International Border to offer ardas and Rehras Sahib prayers for the reopening of the corridor leading to Gurdwara Sri Kartarpur Sahib in Pakistan's Narowal district. According to The Tribune's report, BSF personnel said permission had been granted only for prayers at a gurdwara near the Zero Line and that the group breached protocol by attempting to move further.

Context & Background

The Kartarpur Corridor was inaugurated on November 9, 2019, to commemorate the 550th birth anniversary of Guru Nanak Dev, permitting visa-free travel for up to 5,000 Indian pilgrims a day to Gurdwara Darbar Sahib — the founder of Sikhism's final resting place. Services were suspended on May 7, 2025, after Operation Sindoor, and have not resumed since.

The closure has drawn sustained opposition from Sikh religious bodies. The Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee passed a resolution during its annual budget session demanding the corridor's immediate restoration. An SGPC delegation led by president Harjinder Singh Dhami met Pakistan's Charge d'Affaires Saad Ahmad Warraich in New Delhi seeking more pilgrim visas ahead of the Prakash Gurpurab of Guru Nanak Dev in November. Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said on August 19 that pilgrimage travel is governed by bilateral arrangements and that corridor services continue to remain suspended in view of the prevailing security situation.

Impact & Analysis

The Zero Line ardas was organized as joint religious observance: while the Indian jatha was led by the Akal Takht Jathedar, Pakistan Sikh Gurdwara Prabandhak Committee president and Punjab provincial minister for minority affairs Ramesh Singh Arora announced a Nagar Kirtan proceeding from Gurdwara Sri Darbar Sahib to the Zero Line on the Pakistan side. Rehras Sahib, kirtan and ardas were held on both sides of the fence, with Gurbani Kirtan and Jaikaras from the Pakistan side audible to devotees gathered on the Indian side.

The Jathedar had asked officials to consult their senior officers and permit five Sikhs to proceed to the Zero Line to hand over a Rumala Sahib for the Guru Granth Sahib and siropas for the Panj Piaras to the Pakistan-side sangat. That request was also declined. Speaking to the media afterward, the Jathedar questioned why Sikh devotees were prevented from reaching the Zero Line merely to offer ardas. The sangat raised Jaikaras, Karah Prashad was distributed, and the jatha returned after the prayers.

The episode underscores how the corridor's suspension has become a recurring point of friction between security management at the border and the religious demands of the Sikh community. With the Prakash Gurpurab in November approaching, the visa-free corridor that once carried thousands of pilgrims daily remains closed, and there is no indication from New Delhi of an imminent change in the security assessment.

Diaspora Angle

For the Sikh diaspora in the United States, Canada and the United Kingdom, Kartarpur Sahib is among the most significant pilgrimage sites, and many families plan visits around Gurpurabs. The corridor's closure since May 2025 has cut off the visa-free route that made those trips practical for elderly and first-time pilgrims, making every development on its reopening closely watched abroad.

What's Next

The MEA has tied any resumption to the security situation, which it described in August as unchanged. Religious bodies are expected to keep up the pressure through the November Gurpurab season, when pilgrim demand peaks. For now, the Zero Line ardas — held within earshot of the other side but short of it — stands as the clearest measure of both the demand for the corridor's reopening and the distance that remains.
